transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-10-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Aurelius Infra), Maria Torres (Aurelius Security), Sam Patel (Aurelius CTO)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Redwood walked through Private VPC deployment options: PrivateLink endpoints vs routed NAT egress, design patterns for subnets and cross-AZ KV cache locality, DNS for private endpoints (Route53 Resolver), and runtime considerations (batching, quantization, cold vs warm KV cache). Aurelius asked about KMS, audit logs, and how to minimize latency impact when using PrivateLink.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Kim: All right everyone, thanks for joining. i'm alex, i'm the AE on the account and we have priya who's going to run the deep dive on private vpc networking and runtime impacts. sound good?
[00:08] Priya Shah: hey! yep, i'll jump right in, and sorry if i talk fast, we've got a lot to cover. do you want the quick agenda - networking, private endpoints, dns, runtime perf (kv cache, batching), and security integrations?
[00:18] Jordan Lee: that sounds good. for context, we run a multi-az k8s cluster in AWS, our models will be in a dedicated Redwood private deployment, and our latency target is 100-150ms p95 for single-turn short prompts, but for long-context (8k-16k) we expect higher. also we have strict data residency and cannot route any payloads through public endpoints.
[00:36] Maria Torres: and on security side we need audit logs, KMS for keys, and SOC2 type artifacts; SSO is already in place. also wondering about egress and how traffic flows to redwood-managed nodes if we use PrivateLink.
[00:45] Priya Shah: great, that's the right constraints. ok first topic: PrivateLink vs NAT egress. PrivateLink gives you an interface endpoint in your VPC, traffic stays on amazon backbone, no public internet egress. NATs require egress to our endpoints that could be public unless you use a private endpoint + vpn/peering. PrivateLink is preferred for strict no-public-internet policies.
[01:05] Sam Patel: quick q - does PrivateLink affect latency compared to direct public API? we've seen ~20-30ms overhead for some providers.
[01:12] Priya Shah: yes, there can be a small additional hop, but often it's negligible because PrivateLink stays on the AWS network and avoids internet variability. where latency matters most is cross-AZ routing and ENI warm-up; the main perf hits are if your KV cache is remote from the runtime.
[01:27] Alex Kim: i'll add: we have customers see about 5-15ms difference in p95 in practice for PrivateLink versus public hosted endpoints, but that depends on region, AZ topology, and whether you're hitting a warm KV cache.
[01:39] Jordan Lee: warm KV cache - can you expand? we plan to use prefix caching heavily to reduce repeated costs for common prompts. how is that stored and does it need to be within the same subnet/az?
[01:49] Priya Shah: good question. our runtime keeps KV cache local to the serving node for lowest latency; when you scale across AZs or use cross-az failover, cache hydration is necessary. for Private deployments we can configure cache affinity to a set of nodes in the same AZ; best practice is to colocate request routing and cache if you need low token-level latency.
[02:09] Maria Torres: so for HA if an AZ goes down do you accept the higher latency when warm cache misses hit a remote replica? what's the degradation pattern?
[02:17] Priya Shah: yes, during failover you'll see higher latencies while caches warm - that could be 100-300ms extra for long-context calls initially, depending on model and batch size. our rollout policies include automatic fallback to a compatible model variant in a different AZ but we recommend warming with synthetic traffic for predictable behavior.
[02:34] Sam Patel: about routing - do you want us to set up VPC peering or use PrivateLink and a dedicated ENI per AZ?
[02:41] Alex Kim: PrivateLink with interface endpoints per AZ is the common pattern for enterprise customers: one ENI per AZ, security groups to lock down sources, and you keep traffic on AWS. Peering can work but adds complexity for transitive routing and DNS.
[02:55] Jordan Lee: can you talk about DNS? our apps resolve internal hostnames; if we create an interface endpoint how do we ensure our DNS resolves redwood-internal.example -> private ip?
[03:03] Priya Shah: you can enable the AWS provided DNS for the endpoint which creates an alias in the VPC - or you can use Route53 Resolver endpoints and conditional forwarding. we usually recommend enabling the VPC endpoint-private DNS to get automatic resolution. if you have on-prem DNS, use outbound endpoints and rules to forward redwood domains to the resolver.
[03:22] Maria Torres: audit logs - what do we get for requests that are serviced via PrivateLink? do we still have request audit trails in our tenant?
[03:30] Alex Kim: yes, for Private deployments the control plane still emits per-request audit logs to your configured S3/bigquery or syslog - we integrate with your logging stack. we also provide token-level cost/latency breakdowns as part of the console or export.
[03:42] Jordan Lee: ok good. switching back to runtime perf - batching. how aggressive should we be on batching if we care about p95 latency? we've got mixed workloads: many short single-turn, some long-context batch jobs.
[03:52] Priya Shah: batching is a latency/cost lever. continuous batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token but adds a queuing delay. we expose per-route policies: micro-batching for latency-sensitive endpoints (batch window 1-5ms) and larger windows for throughput jobs. for p95 around 100-150ms, we generally set small batch windows and autoscale to reduce queueing. also adaptive batching works well if you have bursty traffic.
[04:16] Sam Patel: quantization - if we use int8 or gptq profiles to save memory, how much effect on latency/quality?
[04:23] Priya Shah: quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput on some GPUs, but there are tradeoffs: certain models see slight latency improvements, others may have small quality regressions on edge-case prompts. we recommend trying qruning/quant profiles in a staging pilot and measuring downstream evals. for Private deployments we support pinned quantized variants so you can A/B test.
[04:42] Jordan Lee: curious about the network egress IPs - if we do PrivateLink, do we need specific security group rules per ENI or can we lock down by prefix?
[04:50] Alex Kim: you can lock down by security group and source IPs at the endpoint level. PrivateLink gives you an ENI in the VPC so standard security group rules apply. we can provide the required SG rules and port lists; usually it's HTTPS (443) only.
[05:01] Maria Torres: earlier you mentioned KMS - how does key management work for Private deployments? can we bring our own keys (BYOK) and does Redwood access them?
[05:09] Priya Shah: yes, BYOK via AWS KMS/HSM is supported. Redwood's control plane can be configured to use customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption. for private deployments we also support customer-managed HSMs if required; access is via IAM role with strict audit and you get CloudTrail logs.
[05:24] Jordan Lee: any nuance around Route Tables and NAT gateways? we have a nat-gw for outbound updates - do we still need it if we use PrivateLink?
[05:32] Priya Shah: if you use PrivateLink for all redwood endpoints you don't need NAT for calls to Redwood. you may still need NAT for OS package updates or other internet egress. PrivateLink removes the need to route to the public internet for Redwood traffic. just ensure route tables in private subnets allow traffic to the endpoint's ENI.
[05:46] Sam Patel: what about cross-account setup? our infra is in a different aws account than our dev tools - can PrivateLink support that?
[05:52] Alex Kim: yes, interface endpoints can be cross-account; we often set up endpoint services in Redwood account and allow our customers' accounts to create the interface endpoints. we provide the endpoint service name and ARNs and it's a straightforward handshake.
[06:02] Jordan Lee: performance numbers - can you put some ballpark p50/p95 numbers for an 8k context model running on dedicated private deployment with PrivateLink and AZ-local KV cache?
[06:12] Priya Shah: ballpark: for short prompts ( <= 256 tokens ) p50 ~ 30-60ms, p95 ~ 80-150ms depending on model. for 8k context generations, p50 could be 200-400ms and p95 400-800ms - lots of variance. with cache warm and optimized batching you can get consistent improvements. these are rough; we'll put exact numbers after we run your benchmark.
[06:36] Maria Torres: any special considerations for TLS certs on PrivateLink?
[06:40] Priya Shah: PrivateLink terminates at the interface endpoint? actually the TLS still terminates at Redwood, but the traffic stays within AWS. mutual TLS is possible if you need zero-trust between endpoints, or you can use AWS Private CA + Mutual TLS. we can support client certs on top of the interface.
[06:56] Jordan Lee: about KV cache replication - is that synchronous? how do you avoid cache divergence?
[07:02] Priya Shah: KV cache is local (in-memory) and we have an option to use a shared cache service for workloads that require replicated state. shared caches add network overhead; we typically recommend local caches with intelligent routing. replication is eventual for speed; for strict consistency it's heavier on latency.
[07:18] Sam Patel: if we want low-latency inference for a subset of endpoints, can we pin models and nodes to a dedicated pool in our VPC?
[07:25] Alex Kim: yes, Redwood Dedicated/Dedicated-in-VPC allows you to reserve GPU pools and pin model versions. you can also configure routing to prefer the dedicated pool for certain API keys/routes.
[07:35] Jordan Lee: regarding monitoring and traces - can we get distributed traces that include redwood runtime spans?
[07:40] Priya Shah: yes we can emit OpenTelemetry spans or integrate with X-Ray; per-request traces and token-level timing can be exported. we also provide dashboards per-route with latency breakdowns (network, runtime, decoding).
[07:52] Maria Torres: one more security Q - data retention: if a request touches our KMS and logs, how long are payload logs retained and can we disable payload storage?
[07:59] Alex Kim: for Private deployments you control retention via the console; by default we don't persist raw payloads unless you enable request archival for audits. you can also configure redact options to avoid storing PII. we'll share the retention config options in the security doc.
[08:12] Priya Shah: ok quick detour to networking nitty-gritty: recommended pattern is one interface endpoint per AZ, attach endpoint security group that allows your service subnet CIDR, set route tables for private subnets to use the endpoint, and avoid cross-AZ hairpinning. also keep DNS resolver rules so your services resolve the endpoint FQDN to the ENI IPs.
[08:35] Jordan Lee: hairpinning - we had issues where requests from AZ-a to an endpoint in AZ-b added 10-20ms. can we bias endpoints by AZ?
[08:43] Priya Shah: yes, the common approach is to create endpoint in every AZ and use local ENI ip addresses via DNS and client-side affinity. Redwood's smart router can also steer traffic by AZ when integrated with your VPC endpoints. we'll show that in the design doc.
[08:58] Sam Patel: about failure modes - what happens if PrivateLink interface endpoints are accidentally deleted? how do we detect and failover?
[09:05] Alex Kim: we recommend monitoring endpoint health (aws cloudwatch metrics for interface endpoints). as for failover, you can rely on DNS TTLs and create multiple endpoints; our router will fallback to other regions or hosted variants if configured. we also support canary policies so you don't push production traffic to a broken path.
[09:22] Jordan Lee: can we get a sample cloudformation/terraform snippet? that would help.
[09:26] Alex Kim: yes, action item: we'll send terraform and CF templates for endpoint creation + SG rules.
[09:31] Maria Torres: any constraints about ENI quotas? we have conservative soft-limits on ENIs per instance.
[09:36] Priya Shah: interface endpoints create ENIs but you can request quota increases; we also offer cross-account endpoint services which reduce per-instance ENI pressure depending on your architecture. we'll include a sizing guide.
[09:47] Jordan Lee: about the benchmark pilot - i want to see tail latencies for 16k token streams. what's required from our side?
[09:53] Priya Shah: we'll need a staging VPC with endpoints configured, a sample dataset and prompt set, and access to a small set of test keys. we'll run a synthetic load test with variable concurrency and batch windows; you'll get p50/p95/p99 and token throughput.
[10:07] Alex Kim: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[10:12] Priya Shah: recapping: 1) Redwood to share network diagram, terraform templates, and security whitepaper (Alex). 2) Redwood SE to send benchmark plan and runbooks (Priya). 3) Aurelius to provision staging VPC and endpoints and share contact for infra access (Jordan). 4) Aurelius security to list compliance questions (Maria).
[10:30] Sam Patel: looks great. thanks everyone.
[10:33] Alex Kim: thanks all, we'll follow up via email and slack w/ artifacts.
[10:38] Jordan Lee: thanks.

--- End Transcript ---
